abstract: Fabrication of an efficient catalyst for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to valuable products at low overpotential remains a severe challenge. Herein, graphene (GN)/Cu2O catalyst, with an average particle size of 20-50 nm has been synthesized and coated on copper foil. The linear seep voltammetry studies showed that the 0.1 mg of GN/Cu2O loaded catalyst exhibited the highest current density in CO2 saturated 0.5 M NaHCO3 electrolyte. The GN/Cu2O electrode was significantly more active toward CO2 reduction showing a current density of approximately 12.2 mA/cm 2 at 1.7 V versus Ag/AgCl, which is higher than Cu2O electrode (8.4 mA/cm 2 ). Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry analysis of the liquid products revealed that ethanol (~ 0.34 ppm) was found to be the predominant product at -0.9 V with high reasonably Faradaic efficiency up to 9.93%. These results suggest that graphene may be used as a promising non-metallic support for the electrochemical reduction of CO2. ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Carbon dioxide emission into ecosystem is among the main scientific and technical challenges since it contributes significantly to the global warming [1-3]. It is well reported that there was around 3.9% increase of the CO2 concentration in the atmosphere each year [4]. To mitigate the problem, CO2 capturing was the commonly pathway used to prevent a large amount of CO2 to release into atmosphere [5]. Recently, CO2 conversion is considered an alternative route for CO2 reutilization in addition to producing valuable chemicals [6-7] and assist to maintain the basic living environment [8-10]. Varying methods such as; chemical, photochemical, and electrochemical have been carried out for CO2 conversion [11]. Numerous studies revealed that the electrochemical method is a promising for CO2 conversion to valuable chemicals and fuels because of simplicity, environmentally friendly, and product can be selectively controlled [12-15]. Electrochemical reduction of CO2 occurs at large negative overpotentials and is limited by hydrogen evolution as a competitive reaction in an aqueous electrolyte. Hence, an efficient catalyst should be designed to overcome these limitations. Furthermore, the product formed as a result of CO2 reduction depends on nature of electrode material, pH, and electrolyte [16-18]. To date, copper/copper oxides catalysts were extensively investigated for

electrochemical reduction of CO2 [19-23]. Oxygen species in copper (I) increase the number of defect electrons so that CO2 was easily adsorbed onto the catalyst surface; however, CO2 reduction at relatively high overpotentials and poor selectivity towards alcohols over Cu2O catalyst are the major obstacles. Therefore, surface modifications are highly desired [15].
In this study, we evaluate the role of graphene as supporting catalyst for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 in aqueous solution. Graphene provide large surface area for the Cu2O active sites, subsequently enhance the electron mobility which can promote the CO2 adsorption and reduction activity as well [24]. The as-synthesized graphene/Cu2O catalyst not only exhibited high performance for CO2 reduction compared to Cu2O, but also showed good selectivity towards ethanol production. The product yield as well as the Faradaic efficiency (FE) have been investigated.

sections.heading: 2.1. Synthesis of GN/Cu2O
sections.text:
Graphene oxide (GO) was synthesized using modified Hummers , methods as described previously [25]. Cuprous oxide (Cu2O) and graphene (GN)/Cu2O nanoparticles were synthesized according to the method described [26]. A 1 mg/ ml GO stock solution was prepared and sonicated for 2 h. Pipette 3 ml GO and dissolved in 15.1 ml ultrapure water followed by ultrasonication for 30 min. Then 0.45 ml 0.1 M CuCl2 and 0.087 g sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) were mixed with the above solution under vigorous stirring. After that, 0.9 ml 1 M NaOH was added followed by rapid injection of 4 ml 0.1 M hydroxylammonium chloride (NH2OH.HCl) into the

Dried in vacuum oven at 40 o C for 18 hours. Cu2O was also prepared by the same procedure as shown in scheme 1. All above chemicals procured from BDH Chemicals Ltd., and used as received without any purification.

sections.heading: 2.2. Physical and electrochemical test
sections.text:
X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were collected using Rigaku MiniFlex X-ray diffractometer (Japan). Samples morphology were examined with a field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM, Lyra 3, Tescan, Czech Republic), and an energy dispersive X-ray spectroscope (EDX, Oxford Inc., UK) was used for elemental analysis. Raman spectroscopy patterns were analyzed in the range from 500 to 200 cm -1 . High resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) JEM-2100F (Japan) used to obtain images of the as-synthesized samples.
Copper foil (fisher scientific company, 3.38 cm 2 ) was mechanically polished using silicon carbide grain (150 mesh) and ultrasonically rinsed successively in diluted sulfuric acid (Sigma Aldrich). Followed by rinsed in acetone and ultrapure water then dried in nitrogen atmosphere. In the electrode fabrications, 1 mg prepared powder (Cu2O or GN/Cu2O) was mixed with 60 µl nafion solution 5 wt.% (Aldrich) and 1 ml acetone, then sonicated for 15 min. One portion of the suspension ink (100 µl) was dropped on the copper foil and dried under hot incandescent lamp.
The electrochemical experiments were carried out in 0.5 M NaHCO3 (Sigma Aldrich, ≥ 99.5%) electrolyte saturated with CO2 (99.99%) using two compartment threeelectrodes cell separated by a glass frit and connected to a Gamry potentiostat. The

counter electrode used was a Pt coil and Ag/AgCl was used as reference electrodes. Copper modified Cu2O and/or GN/Cu2O electrodes were used as working electrode. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) measurements were carried out in the range from - 0.2 to -1.8 V vs. Ag/AgCl at scan rate of 20 mV/s. prior to measurement, High purity N2 or CO2 (99.99 %) saturated electrolyte solution were employed to evaluate the electrode behavior. Bulk electrolysis of CO2 was performed at different fixed potentials. Prior to electrolysis, electrolyte was bubbled with N2 then saturated with CO2 by bubbling for 30 min. All electrochemical measurements were carried out at ambient conditions. Liquid products were analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GCMS, Agilent technologies). Dichloromethane (≥ 99.9%, GC grade, Sigma Aldrich) was used for liquid products extraction before injection to avoid GC damage. After 0.2 µl liquid sample injection, the oven temperature was held at 40 o C for the first 5 min. Then the temperature was increased to 200 o C at 10 o C/min to remove water. Here, we accounted only for the liquid products. Faradaic efficiency is calculated assuming that 12 electrons are required per ethanol molecule using the following equation: FE (%) = (Z.N.F/q) x 100 Where, Z is number of electrons, n is number of mole produced, and q is the total charge applied during the electrolysis process.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussions
sections.text:
To demonstrate the successful synthesis of Cu2O and GN/Cu2O catalysts, various analytical techniques were employed. The crystal structure of the as-synthesized catalysts were analysed by XRD technique and their patterns are given in fig. 1. It was observed that characteristic peaks appeared at 2 theta angles 36.4 o , 42.3 o , 61.3 o , and
AC C

73.5 o which can be assigned to reflections (111), (200), (220), and (311) cubic crystal structure of Cu2O planes, respectively. These results are agreed with JCPDS card no. 87-2076 [26-27]. According to XRD patterns there were no other peaks detected due to impurities, and the sharpness of pure Cu2O peaks indicates the crystallinity nature. As can be seen in fig. 1, pure Cu2O peaks are sharper and narrower than those of GN/Cu2O which is ascribed to the presence of graphene.
The surface morphologies of Cu2O and GN/Cu2O catalysts were investigated with FE-SEM analysis. Fig. 2 (a) clearly indicated the cubic structure of Cu2O, and the edge length varying from 200- 500 nm. Also, it is apparent that graphene decorated with Cu2O nanoparticles as shown in fig. 2 (b). Additionally, the size of Cu2O dispersed onto graphene layers was reduced to around 200 nm, smaller than that of pure Cu2O. EDX analysis of GN/Cu2O indicated the existence of Cu, O, and C peaks as shown in fig. 2 (c) (Al and Mg peaks are coming from sample holder). The TEM image of GN/Cu2O revealed that the graphene layers were wrapped the Cu2O particles with an average size of 20-50 nm as shown in fig. 3 (a). HRTEM image exhibited a lattice fringe spacing of 0.213 nm in several orientation regions, corresponding to (200) crystal plane of Cu2O as shown in fig. 3 (b). These results are in good agreement with the results obtained from XRD.
Raman scattering is a well-known as an essential technique for carbonaceous materials characterization. Fig. 4 shows the Raman spectra for graphene oxide and GN/Cu2O composite. Two obvious broad G and D bands appeared at 1586 cm -1 and 1350 cm -1
, respectively. Further observation showed that ID/IG ratio for GN/Cu2O

composite larger than that of GO, implying the removal of oxygen functional group in GO during the reduction process [28].
To investigate the voltammetric behavior of the Cu2O and GN/Cu2O electrodes compared with copper foil, in aqueous 0.5 M NaHCO3 electrolytes saturated with CO2 (99.99%), LSV measurements were employed between -0.2 and -1.8 V vs. Ag/AgCl. Fig. 5 demonstrates the linear sweep voltammetry curves of bare Cu foil, Cu2O, and GN/Cu2O electrodes under N2 saturated electrolyte solution to clarify the influence of hydrogen evolution. The potential was scanned at a sweep rate of 20 mV/s. As evident from fig. 5, the current density gradually increased with increasingly negative potential applied to the cathode. Surely, the recorded currents were mainly associated with hydrogen evolution reaction. The obvious cathodic peak near -1.3 V is related to the reduction of Cu(I) to Cu 0 on the electrode surface, while the solution remained clear. As seen from this figure, copper modified electrodes exhibited current density values higher than copper foil. Thus, GN/Cu2O electrode performed better than other electrodes. Fig. 6 illustrates the LSV curves of the electrodes when CO2 is purged. There is no significant change in the voltammograms shape between the electrodes, moreover the onset potentials depends on pH and adsorption/desorption mode at electrode surface. Based on 0.1 mg of loaded material, the current density values at - 1.7 V for GN/Cu2O and Cu2O were 12.2 and 8.4 mA/cm 2 , respectively. Graphene possess high electrical conductivity and increases the available surface area of the catalyst. Therefore, the observed higher current density value for GN/Cu2O electrode is indicative of the graphene enhancement of this electrocatalytic effect. Comparing
with some previous reports for copper-based electrodes, the recorded current value for GN/Cu2O electrode is a promising [27,29-31]. Remarkably, LSV curves shows that the cathodic current at GN/Cu2O electrode in the CO2 saturated is lower than that in

the N2 saturated electrolyte (inset fig. 6). The exact nature of this behavior may coincide with adsorption of some species resulting from CO2 reduction on the electrode surface [27,29]. These results concluded that graphene may be a promising support for Cu2O active sites in catalytic activity toward CO2 reduction.
To demonstrate the performance for GN/Cu2O electrode, electrolysis was carried out at fixed electrode potential for 20 min reduction. In general, the current started at high value and decreased gradually with time as shown in fig. 7. At -0.9 V, the current started approximately at -10 mA and declined slowly to -0.5 mA. Also, at -1.3 V, GN/Cu2O electrode exhibited an initial current value of -31 mA and decreased rapidly to -4 mA after 20 s of electrolysis, then it goes constantly for the remaining time. Earlier studies explained the degradation nature of the recorded current by the detachment of oxide surface [29,32,33].
The liquid product was analyzed by GC-MS after CO2 reduction over GN/Cu2O electrode surface, varying fixed potentials have been tested. Ethanol was found to be the predominant product produced as a result of CO2 reduction (Fig. S1). Furthermore, the produced ethanol is highly dependent on the electrode potential. The Faradaic efficiency for ethanol was 9.93% at -0.9 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) as shown in table 1. Further increase in negative overpotential (-1.3 V) results in a lower Faradaic efficiency due to the prevalence of hydrogen evolution over CO2 reduction. Moreover, at that large potential Cu(I) will be reduced to Cu(0) that might be generate other products but in much smaller quantities beyond the typical detection limits. In comparison, no liquid products were detected at -0.9 V over Cu2O-based electrode under the same reaction conditions. Consequently, these results clearly demonstrate

that GN/Cu2O perform as an efficient and highly selective electrode towards ethanol production.
Whilst the electroreduction of CO2 over various copper-based electrodes have been deeply studied [32,34], however, the catalytic mechanisms proposed are still controversial. We suggest the mechanistic pathways for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol as described earlier [35]. It is well known, the adsorbate *CO species is the first intermediate formed during electrochemical CO2 reduction at relatively high negative potentials [11,36,37]. In a recent electrokinetic study, *CHxO intermediate is favored C-C coupling reaction rather than *CO intermediate [38]. Moreover, graphene enhances the electron transfer mobility over Cu2O surface. As a result, *CHxO adsorbed species can further easily reduced to *C2HxO2 intermediate through dimerization and hydrogenation reactions [20,35]. In addition, the critical role played by the edges formed as Cu + reduced to Cu during CO2 reduction to coverage the surface of *CHxO reactive species and facilitate their dimerization to *C2HxO2 intermediate. Subsequently, *C2HxO2 intermediate undergoes reduction to ethanol. Table 2 shows comparison of Faradaic efficiency for ethanol production over different copper-based electrodes. The Faradaic efficiency of ethanol depends mostly on the thickness of catalyst (material loading) and the applied potential [35]. Therefore, the results presented in table 2 reveal the graphene role in improving the efficiency and selectivity towards ethanol production using 0.1 mg GN/Cu2O catalyst at - 0.9 V (vs. Ag/AgCl).
4. Conclusions

D M

The electrochemical reduction of CO2 using graphene/Cu2O electrode showed a significant improvement in current density due to graphene contribution. Linear sweep voltammetry measurements resulted in a high current density value of 12.2 mA/cm 2 at -1.7 V vs. Ag/AgCl when compared to Cu2O electrode (8.4 mA/cm 2 ). Very low material loading of graphene/Cu2O (0.1 mg) was utilized and resulted in significant conversion of CO2 to ethanol. Ethanol was found to be the predominant liquid product with FE of 9.93% at -0.9 V vs. Ag/AgCl under ambient conditions. No other liquid products were detected which clearly shows the selectivity of the reaction. This was attributed to the graphene role as non-metallic supporting catalyst for the electrochemical reduction of CO2.
